summaries.summary: Pre-trained models attract attention for downstream NLP results, while multilingual models enable zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, including multilingual-BERT on five NLP tasks.
Research emphasizes English pre-trained models, with only three multilingual models available: mBERT supporting 104 languages, XLM supporting 100, and LASER supporting 93.
The work develops energy-efficient transfer of English pre-trained models to other languages by learning target embeddings, fixing encoder layers, and fine-tuning bilingual LMs.
The authors propose fast adaptation producing a bilingual BERT_base of English and a target language within a day using one Tesla V100 16GB GPU.
Bilingual LMs are evaluated for six languages on natural language inference and universal dependency parsing, showing competitive or better performance than mBERT.
The bilingual LMs can serve as an excellent feature extractor in supervised dependency parsing task.
The paragraph defines English word-embeddings, Transformer encoder computations, contextualized representations, and output word prediction for pre-trained LMs.
Autoencoding LM predicts masked original tokens, autoregressive LM predicts next tokens, and XLNet factorizes permutations to capture bidirectional context.
The three-step approach initializes target embeddings, fine-tunes them with the English encoder fixed, then constructs and fine-tunes a bilingual LM.
Foreign word embeddings are initialized by mapping English embeddings so semantically similar foreign and English words have similar embeddings via linear combinations.
The sparse vector alpha_i lies in |V_e| dimensions and its components sum to 1.
Good estimation of alpha_i can speed convergence and enable zero-shot transfer, estimated under parallel English-foreign data or monolingual data scenarios.
With an English-foreign parallel corpus, word translation probability p(e|f) is estimated using word-alignment toolkits such as fast-align.
Because alpha_i is estimated from word alignment, it is a sparse vector.
For low resource languages without parallel data, monolingual data and fastText word vectors aligned with English estimate word translation probabilities.
Sparsemax replaces softmax to assign zero probabilities to most English vocabulary words, improving initialization of foreign embeddings.
After initialization, foreign embeddings replace English embeddings, and only foreign embeddings are fine-tuned on monolingual data using the English LM objective.
A bilingual LM has separate English and foreign embedding and output layers, a shared encoder, and is fine-tuned on both monolingual datasets.
RAMEN bilingual LMs start from BERT_base, BERT_large, RoBERTa_base, and RoBERTa_large, and are evaluated on XNLI and dependency parsing.
Six target languages—French, Russian, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, and Vietnamese—span four language families and different monolingual data conditions.
Parallel data come from United Nations Parallel Corpus, IIT Bombay corpus, and OpenSubtitles 2018, while monolingual experiments use fastText vectors and Wikipedias.
English uses provided tokenizers, while target languages use fastBPE with 30,000 or 50,000 codes and vocabularies of 32,000 or 50,000.
XNLI and Universal Dependencies v2.4 are used, with specified treebanks for English, French, Russian, Arabic, Vietnamese, Hindi, and Chinese.
Although shared subwords improve embedding alignments and mBERT transfer, RAMEN does not share subwords, giving identical subwords different embeddings.
Subword translation probabilities are estimated by subsampling 2M sentence pairs from each parallel corpus and tokenizing into subwords before fast-align.
Subword vectors from aligned fastText word vectors are approximated as weighted averages of word vectors containing the subword.
The top 50,000 words in each aligned word-vectors are used to compute subword vectors, with p(w_j) and n_s defined.
Foreign vocabulary words not initialized from English word-embeddings are initialized randomly from a Gaussian N(0, 1/d^2).
RAMEN_base is tuned for 175,000 updates and RAMEN_large for 275,000, with sequence length 256 and specified mini-batch sizes.
RAMEN_base uses Lookahead wrapped around Adam with learning rate 10^-4, k=5, alpha=0.5, while RAMEN_large uses Adam due to memory limit.
Fine-tuning RAMEN on XNLI and UD uses mini-batch size 32, Adam learning rate 10^-5, 4 and 50 epochs, and one Tesla V100 16GB GPU.
This section presents model results for two zero-shot cross lingual transfer tasks: XNLI and dependency parsing.
Table TABREF32 shows XNLI test accuracy, with the fairest comparison being mBERT versus monolingual-only RAMEN_base+BERT.
RAMEN_base initialized from fastText outperforms mBERT by 1.9 points on average and 3.3 points on Arabic, with further gains from parallel data and RAMEN_large.
RoBERTa transfer improves zero-shot accuracies, with RAMEN_base+RoBERTa exceeding RAMEN_base+BERT by 2.9 and 2.3 points and state-of-the-art results for five languages.
RAMEN currently uses parallel data only to initialize foreign embeddings, and starting from BERT_base yields competitive bilingual LMs with mBERT for zero-shot XNLI.
A graph-based dependency parser is built on RAMEN without part-of-speech tags, feeding contextualized representations into Deep-Biaffine layers for LAS evaluation.
Monolingually initialized RAMEN_base+BERT outperforms mBERT on five languages except Arabic, with +5.2 LAS for French and +3.1 LAS for Chinese.
Randomly initialized foreign embeddings reduce RAMEN_base zero-shot performance by 15.9% for XNLI and 27.8 points for UD parsing versus aligned fastText vectors.
The authors evaluate RAMEN contextual representations as a feature extractor for supervised dependency parsing on UD datasets.
On UD supervised parsing, RAMEN_base+BERT is competitive with mBERT and exceeds it by +1.2 points for Vietnamese, while RAMEN_large+RoBERTa achieves the best LAS.
RAMEN+RoBERTa_base initialized from monolingual data is evaluated at embedding initialization, 25K target-embedding updates, and subsequent 25K-update stages.
Without fine-tuning, average XLNI accuracy is 39.7% and average LAS is 3.6, with the biggest leap after 50K updates and 19-30 LAS gains except French.
Language similarities affect syntax transfer more than semantics, with French reaching 50.3 LAS while Arabic and Hindi reach 4.2 and 6.4 points.
Whether the approach applies to autoregressive LMs such as XLNet remains unresolved and is left for future work.
